segments.say: Last year, people in Singapore lost nine hundred and thirteen million dollars to scams. In four out of five cases, nobody hacks anything. A scammer talks the victim into pressing send.

That is why bank fraud models miss them. They are built to catch stolen cards and passwords, but here the real customer is paying. Police can now freeze a victim's accounts, but only as a last resort: just twelve orders so far. Banks said anything finer-grained would need significant system changes.

ScamBreaker-Z makes that change inside the payment itself, on IBM LinuxONE. Three models score every transfer in milliseconds: the payee's mule risk, this customer's normal behaviour, and signs of coercion in the session. The response is proportionate: allow, nudge, a twenty-four-hour hold, or block.
Here it is, live on our LinuxONE server, scoring IBM's AMLworld transactions at {tps} per second, with a p99 decision latency of {p99} milliseconds.

Mrs Tan is seventy-two. A caller posing as a government officer tells her to move eighteen thousand five hundred dollars to a safe account. {tan_decision} in {tan_ms} milliseconds. IBM Granite, running on the same server, explains why in English and in Chinese, and alerts her daughter.
The analyst sees every reason, which model raised it, and a case summary grounded in our policy documents.
Ravi has been lured into a crypto investment that keeps asking for bigger top-ups. {ravi_text}

Everything runs in containers on IBM LinuxONE. {nnpa_text} Granite runs on the box, on a network with no route to the internet, so customer data never leaves. Data at rest is encrypted by the CPACF crypto unit, and every decision is written to a tamper-evident hash chain.

On held-out test days, ScamBreaker-Z held {scam_usd} percent of scam money while holding only {legit_hold} percent of legitimate payments. Behaviour alone would catch {b_only} percent; adding coercion and payee signals takes it to {scam_usd}.
Detect, decide, respond: inside the transaction. ScamBreaker-Z.
